title: The Westo, Erie refugees who carried the Beaver Wars south
summary: Driven from Lake Erie in the 1650s, the Westo crossed the mountains, traded captives for English guns and held the Savannah River until the 1680 Westo War.
bodyMarkdown:
In the 1650s the [Beaver Wars](https://grokipedia.com/page/Beaver_Wars) reached the south shore of Lake Erie. The Five Nations of the [Iroquois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Iroquois), fighting to control the fur and gun trade, had already broken the Huron and the Neutral, and in the mid-1650s their war parties destroyed the towns of the [Erie](https://grokipedia.com/page/Erie_people). The same wars left the Ohio Valley, Kentucky included, a contested hunting ground for the rest of the century. Many Erie were killed or taken into Iroquois towns. One band went south instead.

## Over the mountains

By 1656 a group of [six or seven hundred](https://www.virginiaplaces.org/nativeamerican/rickahocan.html) newcomers had crossed the mountains and settled at the falls of the James River, near present-day Richmond. Virginians called them Rickahocans or Richahecrians, a name taken to mean people from beyond the mountains. Most historians now identify them as Erie refugees, though some older accounts linked them to the Yuchi.

The Virginia assembly told Col. Edward Hill to move the strangers on peacefully if he could and asked the Pamunkey, [bound by a 1646 treaty](https://www.virginiaplaces.org/nativeamerican/rickahocan.html), to send warriors. Hill attacked instead. At the [Battle of Bloody Run](https://encyclopediavirginia.org/entries/indian-enslavement-in-virginia/) his militia fell back and left their allies to fight alone, and the Pamunkey leader Totopotomoy was killed with most of his men. The creek was said to have run red. The assembly suspended Hill and made him pay for a peace.

## The gun trade

Virginia’s leaders decided that trading with the newcomers paid better than fighting them. Traders such as [Abraham Wood](https://encyclopediavirginia.org/entries/indian-enslavement-in-virginia/) exchanged muskets, powder and shot for captives taken from other Native nations, and the captives were sold into slavery. Armed with guns before almost any of their neighbors, the people the English now called the Westo moved south to the Savannah River. By 1659 Spanish officials in Florida were reporting raiders with firearms supplied from Jamestown.

From [about 1660 to 1680](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/westo-indians/) the Westo lived on the Savannah near present-day Augusta, Georgia. They raided across Georgia, the Carolinas and as far as the Spanish missions of Florida, trading their captives for guns, steel hatchets, blankets and glass beads. They were also known as Chichimecos. Their methods copied the Iroquois tactics that had driven them from home.

When the Carolina colony was founded in 1670, it needed them. In 1674 the trader Henry Woodward [walked back with a party of Westo](https://www.scencyclopedia.org/sce/entries/westos/) to their town on the Savannah and opened a trade in deerskins and Indian slaves. For six years Carolina armed the Westo as a shield against Spain, and they became the best-armed nation in the Southeast.

## The Westo War

The alliance did not last. Private traders wanted the slave trade for themselves, and the proprietors tried to make it a monopoly. In 1680 a group of Carolinians known as the Goose Creek Men secretly armed the Savannahs, a band of [Shawnee](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shawnee) newly arrived on the river, and the Westo War broke Westo power within a few years. Most Westo were killed or captured. Survivors went north to the Iroquois for a time, then settled on the Ocmulgee River in Georgia, where the Creek absorbed them.

The Westo carried the Beaver Wars across the mountains: refugees of the gun-and-captive trade who became its agents in the South. Their story is told here alongside the [Erie](/stories/erie-the-cat-nation/) and the [Iroquois Beaver Wars](/stories/iroquois-beaver-wars/). No place in Kentucky is pinned for the Westo.
Source: [New Georgia Encyclopedia: Westo Indians](https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/westo-indians/)
